slides.title: Transplant rejection and kidney biopsy
paragraphs: A kidney transplant gives a person a donor kidney. The recipient's immune system can recognize it as foreign and attack it. That immune response is rejection.

A kidney biopsy is a small tissue sample collected from the kidney for examination. There are two types of measurement. The first is histology, which is a microscopic examination that reveals injury and inflammation, which can support a rejection diagnosis.

The second is molecular measurements. These are counts of selected RNA types that reflect gene activity in the mix of cells in the tissue. RNA includes messages cells make when genes are active. More immune cells in a specimen can also change its RNA pattern.
This project uses those molecular measurements to compare classifiers and build a scoring application.
actions: Read the definitions in order. Introduce the two types of measurement aloud, then move to the project purpose. Leave the clinical and research context to slide 4.

slides.title: Purpose of this project
paragraphs: Whether rejection is present can affect decisions about further treatment to suppress the immune system. Missed rejection can leave kidney injury untreated, while unnecessary treatment can worsen an infection. A binary molecular score could provide additional evidence during that assessment, while subtype and other findings would still guide treatment.

The first part is model comparison. How do logistic regression and CatBoost compare in classifying any recorded rejection versus no rejection from B-HOT biopsy RNA, particularly in missed cases and incorrect flags? I evaluate them against the recorded diagnoses on the same specimens.

The second part is software engineering. I made preprocessing, training and evaluation reproducible, then built a tested scoring service and prototype application. They let a user submit compatible RNA counts and inspect the selected model score, its threshold and the rejection flag. An analyst can try the model through the application, and other software can call the service.
actions: Connect the binary endpoint to treatment-related assessment and briefly explain both error consequences. Give the model comparison and software aims equal weight. slides.title: Clinical and research context
paragraphs: Banff is a framework specialists use to classify transplant biopsy findings. Its current guidance includes thoroughly validated biopsy transcript tests in defined settings for antibody-mediated rejection. That gives molecular assessment an established clinical context. It does not confer that validation on my classifier.

Zhang and colleagues provide the public B-HOT data. Their four-class study already compared regularized regression with other approaches, including gradient boosting. They selected LASSO, a form of regularized regression, because accuracy was similar and it can use fewer weighted features. Their result is a reason to take the simpler comparator seriously.

Biopsy findings also help guide treatment. KDIGO recommends biopsy before treating acute rejection, unless waiting would substantially delay treatment. This connects the assessment of biopsy findings to a treatment decision. It does not establish that my model improves that decision.
actions: Explain Banff and Zhang, then the Biopsy and treatment row. Expand KDIGO as Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes if needed. Retain the exception for substantial treatment delay. The two error consequences were introduced on slide 3.

slides.title: What the dataset contains
paragraphs: I assembled the public downloads into these two tables. The count table has one row per specimen and 770 RNA measurements. The specimen-information table supplies the recorded diagnosis and study group. Specimen ID joins the rows one to one, so GSM6510425 identifies the same specimen in both tables.

Of the 1,395 specimens, 1,193 are transplant biopsies and 202 are native-kidney controls, meaning the person's own kidneys. These controls include normal tissue, but also inflammation from infection or other disease. They help distinguish rejection from other causes of inflammation, rather than making every inflammatory signal a rejection signal.

That is useful, but it also changes the population being tested. Discovery contains 191 native controls and validation only 11. I included all specimens, and the public metadata do not identify the native controls individually, so I cannot report transplant-only performance.

The paper calls the validation cohort independent, but does not document separation by patient or referring center. The public metadata lack those identifiers, so I cannot verify separation. This does not establish that overlap occurred. All specimens were processed at Arkana Laboratories.

slides.title: Outcome: rejection versus no rejection
paragraphs: Antibody-mediated rejection involves immune proteins called antibodies. T-cell-mediated rejection involves immune cells called T cells. Mixed rejection includes both. I combine those three diagnoses as rejection, against the recorded no-rejection category.

The authors excluded borderline acute T-cell-mediated rejection, where findings are suspicious but fall short of the full criteria, and chronic inactive antibody-mediated rejection. The paper does not report how many cases these diagnostic exclusions removed, so I cannot give a percentage. They matter because the comparison leaves out categories where interpreting the findings can be difficult.
I retained the original diagnoses as well, so I could check where the missed cases occurred.
actions: Show how the three rejection diagnoses share one label. Give the two excluded-category examples aloud. The number removed for these diagnoses is unreported; do not confuse it with the 40 specimens removed after assay quality checks.

slides.title: The measurements used to build the features
paragraphs: Each specimen has 770 counts of selected RNA types. The 758 model measurements include human and viral RNA. Their signals reflect both gene activity and the mixture of cells in the biopsy. Their normalized values become the model's inputs.
The other 12 measure relatively stable housekeeping RNAs. More usable RNA entering the assay can raise counts across many measurements. The reference helps adjust for that overall difference.
I used the housekeeping counts for normalization, then excluded them from the model. The next slide shows the calculation.

slides.title: Preparing counts for the model
paragraphs: For each of the 758 counts, I used the same four steps. The right side follows IFNG in my public example, starting with its raw count of four.
Add one and take the base-two logarithm. Adding one allows zero counts, and the logarithm compresses the range. For IFNG, log base two of five is about 2.322.
Next, do that same transformation for each of the 12 housekeeping counts and average them. In this specimen, the reference is about 7.900.

Subtract that reference from each transformed count. For IFNG, 2.322 minus 7.900 gives minus 5.578. So the final value describes the target's signal relative to the reference level. The same raw count can produce a different normalized value in a specimen with a different reference. Those 758 normalized values are the model inputs.
actions: Walk down the four numbered steps, using IFNG for the arithmetic.

slides.title: Models compared
paragraphs: Each model produces a rejection score. I call it a score because calibration has not established reliable individual probabilities here.
The constant model uses the training rejection fraction for everyone. It shows what happens without RNA measurements.

IFNG encodes interferon gamma, an immune-signalling protein associated with T-cell-mediated rejection. I used logistic regression with this one normalized measurement as a simple benchmark. It was fixed in the starting recipe, rather than selected as the best individual predictor.
The all-RNA model also used logistic regression, but combined all 758 normalized measurements using learned weights. Regularization limited those weights to reduce overfitting.

CatBoost can capture nonlinear patterns and interactions. One RNA measurement's relationship with rejection can depend on another measurement's level. It works with numerical inputs, so categorical features are not required. Shallow trees and a small learning rate help limit overfitting.

The comparison uses the same specimens and normalization. The main comparison is all-RNA logistic regression versus CatBoost, with IFNG and the constant model as supporting benchmarks. I examine how their missed rejection and false positives differ.

slides.title: Selecting the model and threshold
paragraphs: A threshold turns a score into a rejection flag. Recall starts with all cases diagnosed as rejection and counts how many the model flags correctly. Precision starts with all rejection flags and counts how many agree with a recorded rejection diagnosis.
I chose a screening target of at least 90 percent recall, then minimized false positives. ROC-AUC broke ties. This was an experiment choice, not a clinical requirement.

Both models detected 157 of 174 screening rejection cases. CatBoost made five false positives among 89 no-rejection specimens. Logistic regression made six. That one-case difference selected CatBoost under the rule.

I kept the selected model and threshold fixed for evaluation. Screening explains the original selection. The separate validation results show how the models compared afterward. Choosing a threshold does not calibrate the score.
actions: Explain each denominator, then the screening rule and the five-versus-six result. Keep the original selection distinct from the later validation comparison.
visible_cues: Recall = correctly flagged rejection cases / all cases diagnosed as rejection. False negatives are missed cases.
Precision = correctly flagged rejection cases / all rejection flags. False positives are incorrect flags.
Screening rule: detect at least 90% of recorded rejection cases, then minimize false positives. ROC-AUC breaks ties.
Rejection detected: CatBoost 157 / 174; all-RNA logistic 157 / 174.
False positives: CatBoost 5 / 89; all-RNA logistic 6 / 89.
One fewer false positive selected CatBoost. The model and threshold then stayed fixed for evaluation.

slides.title: Validation results
paragraphs: These results use the same 345 validation specimens: missed cases among 169 recorded as rejection, and incorrect flags among 176 recorded as no rejection.
IFNG missed 14 cases and incorrectly flagged 75. All-RNA logistic regression missed 33 and incorrectly flagged eight. CatBoost missed 25 and also incorrectly flagged eight.

CatBoost therefore missed eight fewer cases than logistic regression, with the same number of incorrect flags. That adds evidence in its favor beyond the narrow screening result. The paired 95 percent bootstrap interval for the recall difference includes zero, though, so a dependable advantage remains uncertain.

CatBoost’s narrow screening advantage prompted a follow-up with 20 random discovery splits, keeping diagnosis proportions similar. Each used 630 specimens for training, 210 for screening and 210 for assessment. This procedure used fewer training specimens and revised candidate settings, held fixed across repetitions. Screening chose settings, thresholds and the preferred family. Assessment checked both family winners afterward. The original 345 validation specimens were unused.

Screening selected CatBoost 13 times and logistic regression seven. The preferred model changed with the discovery split, so logistic regression remains a credible simpler alternative. The repetitions reuse specimens.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer incorrect flags but misses 11 more cases. Its validation recall is 85.2 percent, below the 90 percent screening target. The preferred tradeoff depends on how the result would be used.
The constant model flags everyone at its threshold of 0.5. It misses no rejection cases but incorrectly flags all 176 no-rejection specimens.

stops.title: The shared calculation and software checks
paragraphs: The key implementation decision was to share the preparation and prediction code. Otherwise, the application could produce a different result from the analysis even while loading the same fitted model.

On the left, the training procedure reads the RNA counts and calls normalize_counts. On the right, the application entry point calls that same function before it scores the specimen. The twelve housekeeping targets supply the within-specimen reference. The remaining seven hundred and fifty-eight targets become model inputs. Any learned scaling or feature selection is fitted on training data and saved with the model.

The application and command-line interface both use Predictor.predict. That makes the calculation reusable without duplicating it in the browser. The browser handles choosing input and displaying the response. The service handles validation and scoring. The complete code guide is available here, but these are the source excerpts that explain the main decision.

The next view shows how other software can call it. An API is a documented interface for exchanging data. Here the caller sends a CSV to POST /predict. This is the exact public input used in the example, available to download. A laboratory research tool or a batch script could send the same request.

The response identifies the specimen and returns the model score, threshold, rejection flag, model version and expected schema version. Those fields let a caller interpret and record the result. The missing-IFNG response uses HTTP status four twenty-two with a concise explanation and no predictions. The same input rules apply whether the request comes from the page or another program.

The final view shows how I checked agreement. I sent all three hundred and forty-five validation specimens through the HTTP service and compared the responses with command-line predictions and the saved research results. The flags matched, and the score differences were below the tolerance shown here. The check included reordered measurement columns, because valid files should be matched by target name rather than accidental column position.

This is a software consistency check. It does not create another estimate of classifier performance. The saved record identifies the model and source files checked. Other tests cover failures such as duplicate measurements and incompatible model metadata.

For handoff, another developer receives the locked environment, commands to reproduce the analysis and start the service, automated checks, and a tested local container with the research model. The hosted workflow passed for an earlier revision; the application and research-container evidence shown here was recorded locally. A cloud deployment remains future work.

Together, the reports make the analysis inspectable, the application makes the model usable, and the shared code and checks keep the software connected to the evaluated procedure. I will return to the slideshow to close.
